title: Stack a new habit on an old one
description: Attach the habit you want to a habit you already never miss, and let the old one carry the new.

body.heading: Pick a reliable anchor
paragraphs: Habit stacking means borrowing strength from something you already do every day without thinking: brushing your teeth, making tea, locking the front door, feeding the cat. These anchors are gold because they never get forgotten.

Choose one anchor that happens at the right time of day for your new habit. If you want to stretch in the morning, anchor it to something in your morning. If you want to read at night, anchor it to something in your evening.

body.heading: Write the sentence
paragraphs: Turn the stack into one plain sentence: “After I pour my morning coffee, I will read one page.” The word “after” does the heavy lifting. It gives the new habit a specific moment instead of a vague intention to do it sometime today.

Keep the new habit small enough that the sentence sounds easy. One page, two stretches, three deep breaths. A stack that feels heavy will be quietly dropped within a week, and the anchor is too valuable to waste.

body.heading: Let it settle before you add more
paragraphs: Give the stack a couple of weeks to become ordinary before stacking anything else onto it. One solid link is worth more than a chain of five fragile ones.
If the new habit keeps getting skipped, the problem is usually the size or the timing, not you. Shrink the habit or move it to a stronger anchor and try again.

takeaway: After a habit you trust, add one small habit — and let the old one do the remembering.
